newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Violence in south Albania, no word on ceasefire.
newsitem.headline: Violence in south Albania, no word on ceasefire.

text.p: Fresh violence erupted in southern Albania on Saturday as rebels seized a government stronghold, putting newly arrived troops to flight and capturing a general.
In Tirana, the head of an international mediation mission said Albanian President Sali Berisha was still considering whether or not to extend a 48-hour ceasefire due to expire early on Sunday.

In the town of Gjirokaster, 30 km (20 miles) from the Greek border, rebels inflicted a humiliating defeat on government forces as at least 120 army reinforcements fled on foot shortly after landing by helicopter.
"The town has fallen to the people, Berisha's troops have turned tail and are in hiding," rebel leader Omar Litse said.

The head of army reinforcements, General Ali Kontrakou, and his aide Georgi Vinti were captured by rebels, Litse said, adding that documents they were carrying indicated a plan to assault rebel-held Sarande and Tepelene.
One helicopter pilot was shot and captured by the rebels, a Reuters photographer said.
The fall of the last government stronghold in the south gives the rebels control over the region, and is likely to make any attempt by the government to retake it more difficult.

In the port of Vlore, a flashpoint in the volatile south, Italy evacuated 33 Italians and Albanians by helicopter across the Adriatic Sea. Residents of a nearby village said one man was shot by unidentified gunmen.
But the Italian government said it was refusing asylum requests from refugees in southern Albania and would send them back.

In Tirana, former Austrian leader Franz Vranitzky, heading a mission of the Vienna-based Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE), said he had asked President Sali Berisha to extend a 48-hour truce, due to expire at 6 a.m. (0500 GMT) on Sunday.

"He was very open to the idea, and will give it very serious thought, he could even imagine that it could be longer than 48 hours," Vranitzky told a news conference after a second, unplanned round of talks with the Albanian leader.

Greece's Deputy Foreign Minister Yannis Kranidiotis, also helping in mediation, said Berisha "appeared to have a negative attitude initially (about the extension), but I have the feeling he was thinking seriously about it".

Berisha, backed by opposition parties, proclaimed the ceasefire beginning on Friday after troops moved southward under a state of emergency proclaimed by parliament, which is dominated by the president's Democratic Party.
Rebels have rejected the government offer and demanded Berisha's resignation, fresh elections and compensation for savers who lost money in the shady investment plans.

Vranitzky said Berisha had reissued a proposal for fresh elections to be held within 45 days. But he said there was limited enthusiasm for such a time-frame from opposition parties, which say polls are impossible under emergency rule.
The former Austrian leader said there were indications Berisha was prepared to be flexible on the date.

In a thinly-veiled warning to Tirana, Vranitzky said no progress could be made on moves to provide international financial aid to Albania and extend cooperation with European institutions until the violence was ended for good.
The OSCE mission also met members of the ruling Democratic Party and an 11-party opposition grouping committed to forming a broader based government.

Vranitzky's mission was the latest of several Western attempts to mediate an end to the rebellion. Dutch Foreign Minister Hans Van Mierlo, representing the European Union presidency, urged Berisha on Friday to refrain from violence.
